_comment: Expected structure per case for the dictated-transcript task: ONE transcript of a clinician speaking a note aloud, sorted into the same four sections the note-formatting task produces. The OUTPUT contract is deliberately identical - a clinician reads one structure, and a pack that grew a second one for the same encounter would be measuring two answers to one question. What differs is the INPUT, and therefore the prompt: written prose is organised and a dictation is not.
_input: ONE transcript per case, read through the `transcript` documents template rather than the `notes` one - `transcripts/{case}.transcript.txt`. Unlike the note-format cases, these are NOT shared with another task's corpus: there is no written note they correspond to, and inventing one would defeat the point. Case names ARE the transcript filenames, which is the constraint the documents template imposes everywhere in this pack.
_synthetic: THE TRANSCRIPTS ARE SYNTHETIC, on the same terms as the notes. They were written for this corpus to exhibit named dictation failures and are not transcribed from, derived from, or edited down from any real recording. A dictation corpus is the likeliest of all of them to carry a real voice into a public repository, because the raw material exists as audio somebody recorded.
_whatThisTaskAdds:
Everything the note-format task measures, over an input that has five properties a written note does not:
  - ORDER IS NOT MEANING. The plan may be dictated first and the history last. A model that partitions by position rather than by content sorts this corpus wrongly and sorts the written one correctly.
  - THE SPEAKER CORRECTS THEMSELVES OUT LOUD. A dose, a drug, and in one case a whole surgical history are stated and then withdrawn. The withdrawn version is still in the transcript, still quotable, and must appear nowhere in the answer. This is the axis with no analogue in the note corpus and it is the reason the task exists.
  - THE SPEAKER DICTATES MARKUP. 'comma', 'period', 'new paragraph', 'colon' are instructions to a typist. They are inside the spans a model must quote, and deletion-only derivation is exactly the tool for removing them - which is a pleasant accident rather than a design: the rule that stops a drug name drifting also strips a filler.
  - THE SPEAKER TALKS TO THE ROOM. Asides to a typist, to a colleague, and to the door are not clinical facts, and they are phrased in the imperative, which is what a plan item is phrased in.
  - THE TRANSCRIBER MISSES WORDS. '[inaudible]' is where a dose should be. It is not a value, and a model that supplies a plausible one has written a prescription nobody dictated.
_dialogue:
THREE CASES ARE NOT DICTATIONS. tr-en-18, tr-en-19 and tr-es-20 are consultations transcribed as they were spoken, two voices with labelled turns, and they are in this task rather than in a task of their own because the OUTPUT contract is the one a clinician reads either way. What they add is an input where the record's facts are not all in the record-keeper's voice: the presenting complaint is quotable only from the patient, a question puts a clinical term in the transcript without asserting it, and a dose is corrected by the OTHER speaker rather than by the one who said it. The last of those is the interesting one, because prompts/transcript.md - unchanged for these cases, deliberately - states the correction rule as 'the speaker's last word is the only word', which is a rule about one speaker. It happens to land on the right dose in tr-en-19 and it is not the reason the right dose is right.

THE FLOORS BELOW PREDATE THESE CASES. They were measured on the seventeen dictations, so a run over this corpus is being gated on a number taken from a smaller and different one until RESULTS.md carries an entry that includes the dialogues.
_matching: `match` works exactly as in note-format-cases.json: alternatives of AND-groups, compared case- and accent-insensitively against an item's `text`. A medication expectation may also carry `dose`, matched the same way against that item's `dose`, or `doseNull: true` where the speaker names a drug without a usable dose. The dose expectations here are doing more work than in the note corpus: on tr-en-02 and tr-en-07 the WRONG dose is also present in the transcript and is also quotable, so a dose error is a model taking the speaker's first word instead of their last.

_expectKinds.present: An item matching these terms must appear in the named section. The gated denominator.
_expectKinds.absent: No item in the named section may match. Each names a specific trap the transcript lays - a retracted drug, a relative's symptom, a dictated punctuation word, an aside to the typist, or two drug names inside one medication item (see _mergedItems).
_expectKinds.empty: The whole section must be `[]`. Three cases turn on it: a pre-operative dictation that states there is no medication and then stops before anything is decided (two empty sections in one case, for two different reasons), and a telephone call whose patient has no past history at all.

_mergedItems:
Every case naming two or more drugs carries an `absent` expectation whose AND-group is two DRUG NAMES: an item matching both is one item that should have been two. It is here because the first graded run walked straight through the gap it closes. On tr-en-12 the model emitted a single medication item whose `text` named all three drugs and whose `dose` held all three schedules, and it scored 3/3 on the drugs with no dose error - a set matcher looking for 'folic acid' finds it in a merged string exactly as well as in its own item, so the contract's one-item-per-drug rule was unmeasured on the axis it matters most. The schema predicted this and said it could not be enforced: no JSON Schema keyword expresses 'text must be a single drug name'. What a schema cannot enforce, an answer key has to check.

The trap is on ALL SIX multi-drug cases rather than on the one where the failure was seen. A check written only where a model already failed is a check fitted to a run, and it would report nothing the next time the same defect appeared two cases over. It costs nothing when the answer is right: three separate items match no pair.

It changes no denominator. `absent` expectations are not gated items, so item recall stays comparable across the key change and only the hallucination count moves.
_negationLimit: An `absent` expectation cannot catch a NEGATED emission: the matcher refuses a match when a negator opens the clause, so a model that emits 'no fever' as a history item scores as though it emitted nothing. That is correct for measuring recall and it means the traps here are written on UN-negated content wherever possible - a retracted drug, an examination finding, a third party's problem. tr-en-09's negation run is graded by `empty` on history rather than by a list of `absent`s, which is the one expectation kind that catches an invention nobody named in advance.
_provenance: Two checks run on EVERY item, exactly as in note formatting. `quote` must be found in the TRANSCRIPT by literal containment under [clinical.quoteVerification]; `text` and `dose` must be derivable from that quote by deletion only under [clinical.textDerivation]. The transcripts are lower-case throughout, which removes the sentence-initial-capital drift that dominated the note corpus's edited-only failures - so an edited-only failure here is a more interesting signal than it is there.
_floors:
MEASURED. Set on 2026-08-22 from two agreeing runs of Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.official.gguf, constrained, temp 0, over the thirteen transcripts and the tightened key — 95% item recall (73/77), 100% provenance (63/63), 99% derivation (82/83), 0 invented spans. The two runs were on different prompt-cache states and agreed item for item, token for token, so the numbers below are a floor under a reproduced result rather than under a single pass. 

THESE FLOORS WERE RAISED, and the history is the point. The previous set — 80/95/90 — was measured over twelve transcripts at 82% recall and 91% derivation. Adding tr-es-13-control took derivation to 85%, six points UNDER its floor, and the task went red. The defect it exposed was that prompts/transcript.md never stated what language to answer in: a Spanish transcript came back as an English note, and since 'text' is the quote with words deleted, translating every word failed derivation on every item while provenance still read 100%. The prompt now states the rule and carries a Spanish worked example. Derivation went 85% → 99% and recall 81% → 95% on the same weights, and the English cases improved too. The floors follow the measurement; they did not wait for it. See RESULTS.md, 'Dictated transcripts'.
_floorsMargin: Each gate sits a little UNDER what was measured, and the gap is doing a job. At temperature 0 this task is deterministic, so a floor set exactly at the measurement would turn any change at all — a prompt edit, a llama.cpp release that re-tokenises one span — into a failed run rather than a moved number, and the pack would spend its failures on noise instead of on regressions. Item recall 90 under 95 is four gated items of room out of 77. Provenance 95 under 100 is about one item: quote verification is the check this corpus has never failed, and it should stay near the top. Derivation 95 under 99 is the tightest of the four, deliberately — and it has already earned that once. Under the previous prompt it sat at 90 under 91, one behaviour away from moving a long way in either direction, and when a thirteenth case brought a second instance of that behaviour it went six points through the floor and stopped the run. A wider margin would have absorbed the defect silently. Fabrication stays at 1.0: it is not a rate to be traded against, and no run of this corpus has yet invented a span.
_floorsAreNotAmbitions: These are floors under the REFERENCE model, not targets for a good one. 95% recall means four items a clinician dictated are not in the reading, and the four that remain are not rounding: two are an amlodipine the speaker corrected and then lost entirely, and two are sections that should be empty and are not. The Spanish cases now score 15/16 rather than 8/16, which is the language fix and not a change of model — a reminder that a number this corpus reports can be a property of the prompt rather than of the weights. A model that only clears these bars is a model this pack can measure, not one this corpus endorses.

cases.name: tr-en-01-rambling
cases.note: The baseline disorganised dictation. The plan is spoken FIRST and explicitly flagged as such ('plan first because i need to remember it'), the reason for the visit comes third, the history fourth. Nothing is retracted and nothing is inaudible: this case measures sorting by content alone, so a failure here is not confounded with the harder axes below. Two drugs with two doses, and a trailing negation run that belongs nowhere.

cases.name: tr-en-02-self-correction
cases.note: The case the task exists for. Three retractions in one dictation, of three different kinds: a MEASUREMENT corrected ('152 over 94 sorry that's wrong 158 over 94'), a DOSE corrected ('amlodipine 5 mg once daily no actually make that 10 mg'), and a DRUG withdrawn entirely ('add ramipril actually no scratch the ramipril'). The superseded dose is the trap with teeth - 5 mg is in the transcript, quotable, and the speaker even mentions it again afterwards ('she's had 5 before'), so a model that takes the first number gets a citation that verifies perfectly for a prescription that is wrong.

cases.name: tr-en-03-dictated-punctuation
cases.note: The speaker dictates every punctuation mark and every paragraph break aloud, and dictates the section headings too. The whole transcript is one run-on stream of words in which 'comma' and 'period' outnumber some of the clinical terms. Two things are measured: that the content survives the markup, and that the markup does not survive into the items. The `absent` expectations on 'comma' and 'period' are the only place in this pack where an expectation names a word that is not clinical at all.

cases.name: tr-en-04-asides
cases.note: Three interruptions that are not about the patient: the speaker looking for the chart, an instruction to the person typing ('sandra can you fax a copy to the practice'), and someone at the door. The fax instruction is the dangerous one and it is why this case is here - it is an imperative, it names an action, it names a recipient, and it is exactly the grammar of a plan item. A model sorting by sentence shape rather than by subject puts it in the plan.

cases.name: tr-en-05-inaudible
cases.note: Two '[inaudible]' markers, in two places where they mean different things. In the duration ('present now for [inaudible] weeks') it costs a detail nobody grades. In the dose ('furosemide [inaudible] milligrams') it is the whole value, and the expectation is a NULL dose: a model that writes 40 mg has written a plausible number that nobody said, and it will cite a span that verifies. The lay name in the same dictation ('her water tablet sorry that is the furosemide') is the second trap - the speaker names the drug themselves, so there is one furosemide item and no water tablet.

cases.name: tr-en-06-cut-off
cases.note: A dictation that stops. The patient is called away before anything is decided and the speaker says so, then says they will finish later. TWO sections must be empty for two unrelated reasons: current_medication because he takes nothing ('not even paracetamol', which is a negation naming a real drug), and plan because nothing was decided. The plan is the harder of the two - every other case in this corpus has one, and an empty plan on a full clinical encounter is the answer a model is least willing to give.

cases.name: tr-en-07-third-party
cases.note: A home visit with the daughter present, and the daughter has her own problem and her own answer to it. Neither belongs to this record. The second discriminator is a dose that is CONDITIONAL: furosemide is 40 mg now and goes to 60 mg 'if the weight is still up', so the medication list says 40 and the plan says 60 - the same shape as a self-correction and arrived at a different way, which is why it sits in a different case.

cases.name: tr-en-08-discharge
cases.note: The longest dictation in the corpus and the one with the most to sort: an antibiotic SWITCH (intravenous co-amoxiclav to oral amoxicillin) that produces one medication item and not two, three oxygen flow rates that produce none, and a follow-up split between the end of the dictation and an afterthought ('oh and one more thing') that arrives after the speaker has already signed off. The afterthought is the axis this case adds to the note corpus's discharge letter: in writing, a plan item at the end of the document is at the end of the plan; in speech it is after the end.

cases.name: tr-en-09-negation-run
cases.note: A telephone consultation dictated as one unpunctuated run of negatives - five of them in two sentences, with no comma anywhere to break the clause. History is expected EMPTY, which is the only expectation kind that catches this: an `absent` list cannot, because the matcher refuses a match when a negator opens the clause, so a model that emits 'no fever' as a history item would score as though it emitted nothing. The medication is named rather than described ('microgynon'), with no dose stated.

cases.name: tr-es-10-consulta
cases.note: A Spanish dictation with Spanish fillers ('eh', 'o sea'), which are not the English ones and are not removable by a list a model memorised in English. The sections carry English keys over Spanish speech, exactly as the other tasks do. The decimal comma in '2,5 mg' is the second point: it is how the dose is said and written in this language, and a dose normalised to '2.5' is no longer a deletion of its quote.

cases.name: tr-es-11-correccion
cases.note: The Spanish half of the correction axis, and the one that retracts a whole PATIENT. The speaker starts dictating an appendicectomy, realises it belongs to somebody else ('no perdón eso es otro paciente'), and states that this patient has no surgical history at all. The drug correction beside it is a substitution with a stated reason - metamizol replaced by paracetamol because the patient is allergic - so a model that keeps the first drug has put an allergen on the medication list of a patient the transcript says is allergic to it.

cases.name: tr-en-12-structured-dictation
cases.note: The disciplined dictator: headings spoken aloud in order, no retraction, no aside, no filler. The easiest case in the corpus and it is here on purpose - without it every transcript is hard, the tier distribution collapses to 3-5, and a prompt change that helps only the well-behaved dictation would be invisible. Three drugs on three different weekly schedules, and one examination finding ('mild swelling of the left wrist') stated positively so that a history section which absorbs today's examination can actually be caught, which a negated finding could not be.

cases.name: tr-es-13-control
cases.note: The shortest transcript in the corpus and the one the contract loses hardest, which is why difficulty here is not a length. A Spanish routine health check, dictated in one breath: no retraction, no aside, no inaudible span, nothing this corpus already measures. What it has instead is a model that ANSWERS IN ENGLISH. tr-es-10 and tr-es-11 did not catch that - both are long enough that the model stays in the source language - so the `language` axis was measured on two cases that never put it under pressure, and 82% item recall was reported over a corpus that did not test the one property a Spanish clinician depends on. Every `present` expectation below is written in Spanish for that reason: a translated answer misses them without needing a trap of its own, and the derivation check fails on the same items independently, so the failure is visible in two columns rather than inferred from one. Two further defects ride along. THE ASR MANGLED BOTH DRUG NAMES - 'amblodipina' for amlodipino and 'en la laperil' for enalapril - and deletion-only derivation makes the garble the correct answer: a model that silently repairs a drug name has written a prescription the recording does not contain, and the repair is indistinguishable from a correct reading to anyone downstream. THE DOSES ARE SPOKEN, not written: '10 miligramos' is not '10 mg' and '2,5 cada 8' is not '2.5 every 8', and the dose expectations are spelled as dictated so that unit normalisation is a dose error rather than a derivation footnote. Finally the visit has NO PLAN - 'viene para control de salud' is the reason for the encounter and 'esta todo bien' is a finding - so `plan` is graded `empty`, which is what catches the observed failure of filing the reason for attendance as a decision nobody made.

cases.name: tr-es-14-polimedicado
cases.note: Six drugs enumerated in ONE run with no pause between a dose and the next name, which is how a medication list is actually dictated and is the case the Spanish half lacked. What it discriminates is dose-to-drug binding under speed: every drug here has a different dose, so a model that slips by one pairs enalapril with atorvastatina's 40 mg and the error is invisible in the prose. The trailing 'la furosemida se la subimos el mes pasado' is a second mention that must not become a seventh drug.

cases.name: tr-es-15-alergias
cases.note: The Spanish negation case, and harder than its English counterpart because the three exclusions are of three DIFFERENT kinds: amoxicilina is an allergy, ibuprofeno is a drug stopped a year ago, and only azitromicina and paracetamol are prescribed today. A model that reads 'amoxicilina no' as a medication line puts a stated allergen on the list of a patient the transcript says reacted to it. 'amoxicilina' is said twice, which is the trap: repetition reads as emphasis and emphasis reads as importance.

cases.name: tr-es-16-dosis
cases.note: A dose retracted inside its own unit — '50 microgramos perdon en 75 microgramos' — where both numbers are quotable and adjacent, so taking the first is a deletion of the transcript exactly as taking the last is. It is the microgram case the Spanish half lacked, and the unit is the point: levotiroxina is dosed in micrograms and metformina in milligrams in the same dictation, so a model that normalises units has changed a dose by a thousand. 'insulina glargina' is the second axis: one drug whose name is two words. The two conditions are expected in presenting_complaint rather than history: this transcript states them as the reason for attendance ('acude para control de') and carries no 'antecedentes' marker, which is the cue tr-es-10 uses to separate the two.

cases.name: tr-es-17-acompanante
cases.note: Three speakers in one dictation: the clinician, the daughter, and the patient — and the daughter is quoting a FOURTH person, a neighbour, about risperidona the patient has never taken. That is one hop further than the English third-party case, which has a relative speaking for themselves. The daughter's observation is expected in history, not presenting_complaint: it is collateral cognitive history, and tr-en-07 sets the convention that presenting_complaint is the patient's own symptom. What this case discriminates is that her observation is KEPT while her neighbour's risperidona is dropped — both arrive in the same voice.

cases.name: tr-en-18-dialogue
cases.note: The first two-speaker case. Every transcript above it is one clinician talking to a microphone; this is a consultation as the room heard it, turns labelled 'dr:' and 'pt:', and it changes three things at once. THE FACT ARRIVES IN THE PATIENT'S VOICE and in the first person - the presenting complaint is quotable only from 'it's my chest doctor i get this tightness when i walk up the hill to the shops', so the item a clinician reads is derived by deleting words from a sentence the clinician did not say. A QUESTION IS NOT AN ASSERTION: 'any pain in the arm or the jaw' and 'any diabetes' put three clinical terms in the transcript that are asked about and then denied, and a model that harvests terms rather than claims files all three as history. THE THIRD PARTY IS NOW A TURN RATHER THAN AN ASIDE - the sister's diabetes and the husband's heart attack are the patient answering the question they were asked, which is the same trap tr-en-07 lays and laid in the clinician's voice. The lay name is here too ('the little white one'), named by the doctor in the next turn exactly as tr-en-05's water tablet is.

cases.name: tr-en-19-dialogue-correction
cases.note: The correction axis, moved into a second voice, and this is the case the dialogue cases exist for. Every retraction above is a speaker abandoning their OWN words, and prompts/transcript.md is written for exactly that: 'the speaker's last word is the only word'. Here the wrong dose is the doctor's ('you're on metformin 1 g twice daily now') and the right one is the patient's contradiction of it ('no doctor it's 500 twice a day i never went up'). Last-word-wins still lands on 500, but for the wrong reason, and a model that treats the clinician as the authority on the record - which is what a note is - takes the 1 g. Both numbers are quotable and the doctor then restates the corrected one, so a citation verifies either way. Beside it sits a drug the PATIENT reports stopping ('i stopped the gliclazide back in the spring'), a stop stated by the person who did it rather than decided by the person dictating.

cases.name: tr-es-20-dialogo
cases.note: The Spanish dialogue, and it puts the language rule under the pressure the two-speaker input adds rather than repeating tr-es-13. The patient answers in lay Spanish ('el azúcar me lo miran pero dicen que está bien') and the doctor asks in clinical Spanish, so a model that translates has two registers to flatten rather than one. The history arrives as a doctor's question the patient confirms - 'y de antecedentes usted tiene hipertensión y artrosis verdad' / 'sí' - which is history stated interrogatively, the one grammar the dictation corpus never uses for a fact that is true. The daughter's hands and her infiltraciones are the third party, and they arrive in the patient's own turn with no marker that they belong to somebody else beyond the word 'hija'. Ibuprofeno is prescribed today and therefore legitimately appears in both plan and medication, quoting the same span.
